newsitem.title: GERMANY: Do business in euros, pay tax in marks, Bonn says.
newsitem.headline: Do business in euros, pay tax in marks, Bonn says.

text.p: If you run a German company, you can do business in euros as soon as European monetary union, planned for 1999, begins. But you will have to pay taxes in marks on any profits you earn during 2001.

That is the state of planning on the switch to the euro, which is scheduled to be issued in notes and coins on January 1, 2002, according to an interim report approved by Chancellor Helmut Kohl's cabinet on Monday.

Germany is looking beyond the heated debate on EMU's (economic and monetary union) starting lineup and timetable. It wants "no obstacle, no compulsion" to be the guiding principle in the three-year transition following the launch of the euro as a book-keeping unit.
"Nobody will be compelled to use the euro," Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt said. "But no-one will be prevented from using the euro if he agrees with his business partner."

Some aspects of the transition have already been settled at international level. For example, the European Union's council of ministers decided in 1995 that governments must issue securities in euros from 1999 onwards.
But other elements of the changeover have been left to national governments to work out. Thus, Germany must pass a law on how old government debts can be switched.
"It is not completely clear what scope legislation must have. We must clearly weigh up the interests of borrowers and holders of debt," the report, by a working group, said.
In practice, the more flexible private sector will outpace lumbering government institutions in making the switch to the new European currency.
Companies should be able to convert their equity into euro-denominated, or even nominal-value-free, shares from 1999 on.
That will avoid converting shares with a typical five mark nominal value into an awkward sum of euros at the prevailing rate at which national currencies are "locked".

The Bundesbank will operate all internal accounts in euros from 1999 onwards. Private sector banks carrying out operations with the central bank will be able to opt to continue to do so in marks or move over to euros.

Germany's public sector lags the Netherlands, Belgium and Ireland in readying the tax system for the euro. Germany, on cost and feasibility grounds, will need until 2002 to switch the tax system over to using euros.
Due to "significant transitional problems" the social security system will use the national currency until 2002.
Bonn, however, wants to make the quickest possible shift after the launch of cash euros in 2002 towards eliminating the double-pricing of goods in shops.
The 1995 EU summit in Madrid left a six-month window open for marking up shop goods in both euros and national currencies, but the report said this would create significant extra costs for retailers.
Opting for a pragmatic solution, the report said: "Double pricing should be avoided where it leads to excessive costs.
"On the other hand, the government and businesses want to retain price transparency during the changeover." Solutions were being examined, the report said.
Also under consideration is a "big bang" switch to having euros circulating in the economy, rather than having cash marks and euros circulating in parallel for up to six months.
Around three quarters of Germans regularly express their opposition to EMU in opinion polls, but the government said their fears were misplaced.
"The introduction of the euro is not a currency reform, but a changeover: The numbers change but the value remains the same," the Finance Ministry said.
